content: The certainty of the evidence regarding the impact of food marketing to which children are exposed was generally rated as low or very low. This low certainty was often attributed to significant or very significant risks of bias in the included studies, as well as serious or very serious inconsistencies in the observed effects. To improve the certainty of evidence, future studies should address common methodological issues, such as failing to account for non-respondents or not controlling for confounding factors in studies examining the impact of food marketing on children. The inconsistency in the effects observed in studies evaluating the effectiveness of policies aimed at restricting food marketing to children can be attributed to variations in study design, sampling methods, and measures of effect. Standardized monitoring procedures could help reduce these inconsistencies and enhance the reliability of the evidence. For example, tools proposed by the WHO Regional Office for Europe and the International Network for Food and Obesity/Non-communicable Diseases Research, Monitoring, and Action Support (INFORMAS) could be utilized to standardize monitoring efforts. As digital marketing, including programmatic advertising and user-generated content, becomes more prevalent, it is essential to develop and use tools to monitor such marketing. The WHO Regional Office for Europe has developed the CLICK tool for monitoring digital food marketing, which should be considered for broader application. Many studies included in systematic reviews on the effectiveness of policies to restrict food marketing to children lacked effect estimates and/or p-values. This limitation prevented pooled analyses, necessitating the use of vote counting based on the direction of effect, which does not provide information on the magnitude of the effect or account for differences in study sizes. Future research should include effect estimates and p-values to enable more robust analyses. Both systematic reviews highlighted the lack of data disaggregated by socioeconomic status (SES), sex, gender, and rurality, which prevented analyses of the impact of food marketing and related policies on health equity. Future studies should aim to include such disaggregated data to facilitate a more detailed examination of the effects on health equity and the effectiveness of policy design elements, such as enforcement mechanisms. Implementation research should address both the processes of policy implementation and the contextual factors that influence these processes. Integrating implementation research into policy and programmatic decision-making from the outset can foster collaboration between policymakers and researchers, ensuring that the research is relevant and actionable. Qualitative comparative analysis can provide further insights into the regulatory governance conditions that lead to effective food environment policies, which in turn can improve population nutrition outcomes. Systems thinking can be a valuable approach for generating robust evidence on the most effective policies. This approach is applicable across the policy-making process, from problem identification and policy analysis to policy evaluation after implementation. The dissemination of guidelines to restrict harmful food marketing to children will be facilitated through WHO regional and country offices, collaborating centers, United Nations partner agencies, civil society organizations, and relevant nutrition webpages. These guidelines will also be shared at global, regional, and national meetings to support policy dialogues aimed at accelerating action to combat obesity. The guidelines are part of a technical package designed to support the implementation of recommendations for preventing and managing obesity across the life course. The impact of these guidelines can be evaluated by assessing their adoption and adaptation across countries. Global-level evaluation will be conducted through periodic Global Nutrition Policy Reviews and the WHO NCD Country Capacity Survey, with findings published in the WHO Global database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA). GINA serves as a centralized platform for sharing information on nutrition actions implemented worldwide, including programmatic details, country-specific adaptations, and lessons learned. In line with the WHO handbook for guideline development, the recommendations in these guidelines will be regularly updated based on new data and information. The WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety will coordinate these updates, following formal procedures outlined in the handbook. When the guidelines are due for review, WHO will welcome suggestions for additional questions to address. If concerns arise about the validity of the recommendations, the Department will communicate this information, along with plans for updates, to relevant stakeholders through announcements on its website and mailing lists, as well as direct communication when necessary.
